Book IV of Marcus Aurelius' Meditations. These passages reflect on the inner retreat of the soul, the common reason shared by all humans, and the Stoic understanding of death and change.

## The Inner Governing Faculty

The inward governing part, when it is in its proper and natural state, stands so disposed towards whatever happens that it always, with ease, adapts itself to what is possible and given. It does not cling absolutely to any one object, but pursues its primary objects with a reservation, and then turns whatever comes in its way into material for itself. It is like fire: a small flame would be extinguished by things thrown upon it, but a bright fire quickly assimilates what is heaped on it and, burning through it, rises still higher from those very things.

Let nothing be done rashly or at random, but everything according to the most precise rules of the art.

## Retreating Into Yourself

Men seek out retreats for themselves: country houses, sea-shores, mountains. And you yourself have been wont to desire such things. But this is altogether the mark of a person of the most ordinary sort. For at whatever hour you choose you may retire into yourself, and nowhere is there any place to which a man may retreat more quietly or with more freedom from the crowd than his own soul — especially if he has within him the kind of thoughts into which he can at once by looking therein find perfect ease; and I mean by ease nothing else than good order. Afford yourself then this retreat continually and refresh and renew yourself.

Let these thoughts be brief and fundamental; something that as soon as you recall them will suffice to wash away all the distress, and send you back to the things you return to. For what is it that you are displeased at? The wickedness of men? Call to mind the conclusion that rational beings are made for one another, that patience is a part of justice, and that men do wrong without intending it. And think how many who once hated, suspected, and fiercely contended with others are now stretched out and turned to ashes.

Or is it the portion allotted to you by the whole that displeases you? Recall the dilemma: either Providence or atoms — and with it all those proofs that the world is as it were one city. But can bodily things affect you still? Consider that the understanding, when it once has collected itself and recognised its own power, does not intermingle with the breath whether it moves smoothly or roughly. And as for fame, think how quickly all things are forgotten, how vast a chaos of infinite time lies on either side, how empty is the echo of applause, how undiscriminating and unstable are those who seem to praise you, and how narrow the space in which it is all confined. For the whole earth is a point, and of it the inhabited quarter is but a very small corner.

## Common Reason and the City of the World

If the faculty of understanding is common to us all, then the reason too — the faculty by virtue of which we are rational — is common. If reason is common, then the reason that commands what is to be done and what is not to be done is common. If that, then law is common. If law, then we are citizens. If we are citizens, we share in some common constitution. If that, then the world is as it were a city. For of what other common constitution can the whole race of mankind be said to be members? From this common city it is that understanding itself, reason, and law come to us. Where else should they come from? For just as the earthy element in me has its source in some earth, and the moist in some other element, and the breath in some source, and the warm and fiery likewise — for nothing comes from nothing, as nothing passes into nothing — so too the intelligent part must have some origin.

## Death as Natural Change

Death is what birth is: a secret of nature; a combination of elements, dissolved again into the same elements. In general it is not a thing of which any man should be ashamed; for it is not out of the course of a rational animal, nor yet contrary to the reason of our constitution.

Such things from such people must necessarily come about; he who wishes otherwise wishes the fig-tree to produce no sap. In general remember that within a very short time both you and he shall both be dead, and after a little while more neither your names nor his shall be remaining anywhere.

## On Opinion and Harm

Take away your opinion, and the complaint is gone: "I have been hurt." Take away the complaint "I have been hurt," and the hurt itself vanishes. That which does not make a man himself worse than he was, neither makes his life worse, nor does it harm him either from without or within.

Whatever happens in the world happens justly; you will find this if you look carefully. I say not only that it happens in a connected series, but also that it happens according to justice, as if assigned by someone distributing according to worth. Keep this under observation as you have begun, and in whatever you do, do it in conjunction with this — the being of a truly good man in the genuine sense. Preserve this in every act.

## The World Is Change

Things of the world are veiled in such obscurity that many philosophers — and not those of the most ordinary sort — have found them altogether inconceivable. And the Stoics themselves find them hard to grasp. What then remains? Only this: that you comfort yourself, and await the natural dissolution, not troubled at the delay, and rest upon these two things only. First: nothing shall happen to me which is not consonant with the nature of the universe. Second: it is in my power to do nothing contrary to my own god and genius — no man can compel me to transgress against it.

This world is mere change, and this life, opinion.
